paper_metadata.title: Quantum Architecture Search for Quantum Monte Carlo Integration via Conditional Parameterized Circuits with Application to Finance

summary: This paper proposes a genetic search method for parameterized quantum circuits to approximate payoff functions for quantum Monte Carlo integration / amplitude estimation in finance. It reports a European call PQC with 8 trainable parameters, a fixed-weight basket CPQC with 92 CNOTs and depth 151 at n=14, and a variable-weight basket circuit, all evaluated on noiseless simulation rather than on hardware.

experiments.description: Genetically trained parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) for European vanilla call option payoff approximation, and its conditional parameterized quantum circuit (CPQC) version used for quantum Monte Carlo integration / amplitude estimation subroutines.

algorithm.variant: PQC-trained function approximation with genetic structure learning; CPQC conversion for AE subroutine
algorithm.ansatz: custom parameterized quantum circuit with alternating encoding and parameterized blocks; hardware-native gates allowed
algorithm.optimizer: PennyLane Root mean squared propagation optimizer
algorithm.convergence_criteria: structure search over 20 generations with 20 iterations per generation; accept new structure if cost decreases, or with probability exp(-5(c_new-c_old)/c_old) if cost increases

problem_formulation.encoding_details: asset price discretized into 2^n values; input x encoded through rotational gates in the PQC and through control-register basis states in the CPQC
problem_formulation.objective_function: approximate payoff f_+(X)=max(X-K,0) for a European call option

problem_instance.description: Pricing a European vanilla call option payoff function

dataset_specification.description: discretized asset prices shown in Example 6 / Fig. 3; values in the paper include 70, 80, 90, 100, 110, 120, 130 on the x-axis and a 3-qubit control register example with x_i in {0,0.1,...,0.7}

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: asset price discretization for quantum Monte Carlo integration; scaling to [0,2π) mentioned for general setup
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: function approximation visual comparison against true payoff; resource comparison against IBM quantum arithmetic implementation across control-qubit sizes

hardware.transpilation_target: CNOT and U(θ,φ,λ) decomposition for resource counting

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: classical pretraining / genetic structure search on a dual Intel Xeon Gold 6240R system with 48 cores
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: discounting of expected payoff applied classically
implementation_details.total_execution_time: about 5.5 hours for the whole genetic training procedure

speedup_claims.conditions: assuming amplitude estimation subroutine and efficient function implementation on a quantum computer
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper claims the usual AE-based quadratic convergence improvement in number of simulations; the experiment itself is a function-approximation / resource comparison, not a full end-to-end pricing speedup demonstration.

speedup_claims.factor: fewer quantum resources than previous quantum arithmetic approach
speedup_claims.conditions: for the trained European call CPQC and the reported resource-count comparison
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the CPQC uses a fraction of the quantum resources compared to bitwise algorithms, but does not provide a single universal speedup factor in the text.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: CPQC gate complexity O(n) for control-register size n; compared against O(n) quantum arithmetic for vanilla option implementation
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: classical Monte Carlo convergence O(1/sqrt(N)) for N simulations

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: CPQC gate complexity is O(n) in the number of control qubits; the paper compares against an O(n) quantum-arithmetic baseline for option pricing, not a demonstrated classical runtime advantage.
limiting_factors: Only noiseless simulation / automatic differentiation used
Quadratic AE speedup is theoretical and not benchmarked against a classical solver
Classical pretraining cost is substantial (about 5.5 hours)
Data loading and circuit synthesis overhead remain significant

notes: No real QPU is used for the PQC/CPQC experiments; the paper states gradients were calculated by automatic differentiation, implying noiseless simulation. The exact qubit count and depth of the trained call-option PQC are not explicitly stated in text, though the circuit figure shows 1 target qubit plus an unspecified number of control qubits.
The paper explicitly reports 8 trainable parameters for the call-option PQC (Fig. 4).
The paper presents a function-approximation circuit for a European call and a CPQC resource comparison, but no empirical quantum-vs-classical advantage is demonstrated.

experiments.description: Genetically trained PQC and CPQC for European basket option with fixed weights, compared to IBM-style quantum arithmetic implementation.

algorithm.variant: PQC-trained basket-option payoff approximation with fixed weights; CPQC conversion for AE subroutine
algorithm.ansatz: custom parameterized quantum circuit with rotational encodings and trainable blocks
algorithm.optimizer: PennyLane Root mean squared propagation optimizer
algorithm.convergence_criteria: same genetic-optimization procedure as exp_1; accept new structure if cost decreases or probabilistically if cost increases

problem_formulation.encoding_details: two underlying assets encoded on separate registers; CPQC adds control-register basis encoding of discretized values

problem_instance.description: Pricing a European basket call option with fixed weights

dataset_specification.description: two underlyings X=(X^(1),X^(2)); weights w=(2/3,1/3); paper notes for n=14 the CPQC has CNOT count 92 and depth 151

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: each underlying represented by its discretization on a separate qubit register; same discretization required for quantum arithmetic baseline
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: function approximation comparison and resource scaling comparison versus IBM quantum arithmetic implementation

hardware.transpilation_target: CNOT and U(θ,φ,λ) decomposition for resource counting

implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: discounting of expected payoff applied classically

speedup_claims.conditions: assuming amplitude estimation and efficient function implementation
speedup_claims.caveats: This is the standard AE claim; the experiment focuses on resource comparison and function approximation.

speedup_claims.conditions: for basket option payoff implementation with fixed weights
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper claims the CPQC gate complexity is linear in the number of control qubits, compared with O(n log2 n) for the quantum arithmetic baseline.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: CPQC gate complexity O(n) in the number of control qubits n; quantum arithmetic baseline O(n log2 n)
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: classical Monte Carlo convergence O(1/sqrt(N)) for N simulations

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: CPQC gate complexity is O(n), while the compared quantum-arithmetic baseline is O(n log n); this is a resource-scaling comparison, not a demonstrated end-to-end advantage.
limiting_factors: No classical baseline runtime comparison for the basket task
Only resource counts and approximation plots are shown
Quadratic AE framing does not establish practical advantage
Classical preprocessing/training overhead is not negligible

notes: The paper explicitly reports the CPQC resource point for n=14 as CNOT count 92 and depth 151, but does not give a full qubit count for the trained basket circuit in text. The circuit figure indicates multiple registers, but the exact total is not stated in the prose.
The comparison baseline is a classical/quantum-arithmetic method from IBM/Qiskit; only the CPQC experiment is extracted here.
The paper reports CPQC resource counts for the fixed-weight basket option, including 92 CNOTs and depth 151 at n=14, but does not demonstrate practical quantum advantage.

experiments.description: Genetically trained PQC and CPQC for European basket option with variable weight as an input feature.

algorithm.variant: PQC-trained basket-option payoff approximation with variable weight input; CPQC conversion for AE subroutine
algorithm.ansatz: custom parameterized quantum circuit with rotational encodings
algorithm.optimizer: PennyLane Root mean squared propagation optimizer

problem_formulation.encoding_details: two asset values plus one weight input encoded through rotational gates; paper notes the variable weight w1 is encoded once at the start of the circuit
problem_formulation.objective_function: approximate basket payoff with variable weight, enabling pricing for different weights or state-dependent weights

problem_instance.description: Pricing a European basket call option where the first asset weight is an input feature

dataset_specification.description: inputs are two asset values and one weight parameter; figure A.5 shows three example weights w1=0, w1≈0.37, w1≈0.74

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: visual comparison of circuit output against true payoff function for several weights

speedup_claims.factor: linear in the number of state qubits
speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical monte carlo / direct function implementation
speedup_claims.conditions: for CPQC construction from a trained PQC with rotational encodings
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the CPQC gate scaling is linear in the number of state qubits needed to represent the securities; no explicit runtime or error benchmark is reported for this variable-weight case.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: CPQC gate complexity linear in the number of state qubits needed to represent the securities X(i)
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: classical Monte Carlo convergence O(1/sqrt(N)) for N simulations

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: The variable-weight basket CPQC is described qualitatively as linearly scalable in control-qubit count, but no quantitative benchmark or runtime comparison is provided.
limiting_factors: No quantitative resource table for the variable-weight case in the prose
Only a trained circuit figure is shown
Advantage is asserted only as a potential future use case

notes: The paper states the variable-weight CPQC is straightforward to construct from the trained PQC because all encoding blocks are rotational gates, but does not provide a full qubit count or depth in text. The figure shows the circuit structure and 16 trainable parameters (Fig. A.5).
The paper states that the variable weight is encoded once and that the resulting CPQC scales linearly, but this is a design claim rather than a demonstrated advantage.
